To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the large increase of the isotope exponent in the underdoping regime of YBCO can be understood in terms of the formation of a charge order gap, and (ii) a similar explanation can be given for the behavior of α near the doping ⅛ of La2CuOy.

(a) the isotope effect coefficient has a minimum at optimum doping in the cuprates and increases strongly towards the underdoping region, and (b), this behavior is explained by the shift of the electronic spectral density from the low-energy region to the high-energy region, and the formation of gaps in the spectral density due to a competing phase, and the small electron– phonon coupling constant obtained from LDA.

the isotope effect on Tc in cuprates is strongly affected by the competition between superconductivity and charge order and that the large increase in α towards the underdoping side is compatible with the weak electron-phonon coupling obtained from LDA calculations.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the isotope effect is not a reliable indicator of the superconducting pairing mechanism in the cuprates.

the isotope effect in cuprate high-temperature superconductors is not a simple measure of the electron-phonon interaction, but rather it reflects the competition between superconducting and charge order tendencies in this family of materials.
the electron–phonons are not important for the high-Tc superconductivity of cuprates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the isotope effect is a powerful tool for studying the physics in the cuprates, but that the isotope exponent is not a good measure of the electron–phonons coupling strength.
the isotope effect in the cuprates can be explained without invoking large electron–phonon matrix elements.
a strong isotope effect on Tc is a necessary but not sufficient criterion for superconductivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the electron–phonons are not the only source of isotope effect in cuprates, and that the effect of the charge order on the isotope effect should be taken into account.
the anomalous behavior is not a signature of strong electron–phonon interactions, but of a competing phase.
a small electron–phononic interaction can lead to a large isotope effect on Tc.
